items.summary:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

assoc_array: don't chain a new shortcut onto an existing one

When a full node's leaves and the new key all share the node's segment,
assoc_array_insert_into_terminal_node() replaces the node with a
shortcut to a pair of new nodes.  If the node is itself the target of a
shortcut, the new shortcut is installed as that shortcut's next node,
and a shortcut leading to a shortcut is something nothing expects:
assoc_array_walk() indexes the second one as a node, and
assoc_array_apply_edit() hits the BUG_ON() in the loop that adjusts
nr_leaves_on_branch, on that same insertion.

Deletion gets a node there.  When the subtree below a shortcut shrinks
enough, assoc_array_delete() collapses it into one node below the
shortcut, and the leaves it collects can all share that node's segment.
The next key that shares it too takes this path.  Eighteen insertions
and a deletion are enough: sixteen keys that agree on bits 0-11, one
that leaves them at bit 8 and is deleted again, and one more that agrees
with the sixteen.

Have the new shortcut replace the one in front of the node as well.
assoc_array_insert_shortcut() gives it that shortcut's back pointer and
parent slot, so the caller installs it where that one was, and excises
the old shortcut along with the node, which takes a second entry in
excised_meta[].  The new shortcut's index key comes from the new key up
to the new skip level, so it covers what the old one did.

Found by a userspace test doing random insertions and deletions on keys
that share long prefixes; a targeted case builds a shortcut, deletes
down to the collapse and inserts one more key.

items.summary:
In the Linux kernel, the following vulnerability has been resolved:

assoc_array: keep gc's cleanup out of the live tree on allocation failure

assoc_array_gc() builds a copy of the tree.  Where the copy reaches a
shortcut, it allocates the copy of the shortcut with kmalloc_flex(),
fills it with memcpy(), links it into the new tree, and only then
allocates the copy of the node after it.  The memcpy() leaves the new
shortcut's next_node pointing at the old tree's node, so if that second
allocation fails, the cleanup, assoc_array_destroy_subtree() on the new
tree, follows the new shortcut into the old tree, and the BUG_ON() on
the old node's back pointer fires.

Allocate the node first, and the shortcut once the node exists, freeing
the node again if the shortcut cannot be allocated.  A copied shortcut
is then only linked into the new tree when the copy of its node is there
to follow it.  Nothing else changes: with no allocation failing, the
trees gc builds are the same as before.

Found by a userspace test that makes each allocation of each operation
fail in turn.

items.summary: A flaw was found in Cockpit. An unauthenticated remote attacker can exploit this vulnerability by initiating and sustaining numerous simultaneous connections to the `cockpit-tls` service. This forces the service to create an unbounded number of detached threads, consuming system resources such as memory and file descriptors. The primary consequence is a denial of service (DoS), leading to degradation or complete unavailability of the Cockpit service for legitimate users.

items.summary:
A flaw was found in the interaction between systemd-gpt-auto-generator and 
confidential computing guest VM images in OpenShift Sandboxed Containers 
(confidential peer pods). systemd-gpt-auto-generator automatically discovers 
and mounts GPT partitions by type GUID at boot with no user confirmation. In 
the confidential computing threat model, where the host/hypervisor is the 
adversary, a malicious host can inject partitions into the guest's virtual 
disk. Most critically, injecting a swap partition causes the guest kernel to 
page out TEE-encrypted memory to a host-controlled block device, breaking the 
confidentiality guarantee of the hardware TEE (AMD SEV-SNP, Intel TDX).

The PodVM images use a GPT-partitioned disk with dm-verity on the root 
partition. However, the roothash= kernel parameter only disables root 
auto-discovery — non-root partitions (swap, /home, /var, /srv, /var/tmp) are 
still auto-discovered and mounted. The generator is shipped unmasked in the 
RHEL systemd-udev subpackage, and no kernel command line parameter in the 
measured UKI addon disables it. Additionally, the PodVM measurement script 
captures PCRs 3, 9, 11, and 12, but not PCR 5 (GPT partition table), so 
partition table modifications are not detected by remote attestation.

items.summary: A flaw was found in xdgmime. A heap-based buffer overflow can be triggered in _xdg_mime_magic_parse_magic_line() in the xdgmimemagic.c file on little-endian systems when an attacker-controlled MIME magic file in a user-writable XDG data location (e.g., in the $XDG_DATA_HOME/mime/magic path) is parsed by an application performing MIME type detection (e.g., via g_content_type_guess()). When performing byte-swap, incorrect pointer arithmetic on the write side causes an out-of-bounds write of 2 bytes, resulting in an application crash or memory corruption.

items.summary: A flaw was found in gnome-remote-desktop as shipped in Red Hat Enterprise Linux. In the VNC TLS I/O handlers, retryable GnuTLS results (GNUTLS_E_AGAIN and GNUTLS_E_INTERRUPTED) are handled with an unbounded busy loop instead of yielding to the event loop. A remote attacker who can reach an enabled VNC TLS listener can cause the event-loop thread to spin at high CPU with no forward progress, resulting in denial of service.

items.summary: A flaw was found in QEMU. If the QIOChannelWebsock object is freed while it is waiting to complete a handshake, a GSource is leaked. This can lead to the callback firing later on and triggering a use-after-free in the use of the channel. This can be abused by a malicious client with network access to the VNC WebSocket port to cause a denial of service during the WebSocket handshake prior to the VNC client authentication.
